RPM vs CPM: What Creators Actually Earn

CPM and RPM sound alike and are routinely confused. The difference decides how much money actually lands in your pocket.

The one-line difference

MetricWho pays / who earnsFormulaTypical (YouTube, 2026)
CPMWhat advertisers pay per 1,000 ad impressions(ad spend ÷ impressions) × 1,000$4–$20 by niche
RPMWhat you earn per 1,000 views, after YouTube's 45% share(revenue ÷ views) × 1,000$1–$17 by niche

A $10 CPM does not become $10 of your money. YouTube keeps 45% of long-form ad revenue (creator share 55%), and not every view is monetized (ad blockers, Premium, limited-ads videos). That is why a channel can see a $20 CPM in Studio and an RPM closer to $5.

The conversion

RPM ≈ CPM × monetized share × creator share. Example: $10 CPM, 60% monetized views, 55% creator share → $10 × 0.60 × 0.55 = $3.30 effective RPM.

Why creators should negotiate with RPM

When a brand offers you a sponsored video, quote your real RPM (total revenue ÷ total views × 1,000), not the CPM shown in YouTube Analytics — Studio's CPM is a platform-wide average, not your rate. Misquoting is a common and costly mistake.

Short-form is a different game

YouTube Shorts, TikTok Creator Rewards and Instagram Reels pay far less per 1,000 views ($0.02–$1.00) because of pooled revenue models and lower advertiser demand. See the Views to Money calculator for platform-agnostic math.
